Typing a note on the sales dashboard lags, so a pull request titled "perf: memoize everything" lands. It wraps every derived value in

, thirty changes in all. The React Profiler tells the same story before and after: each keystroke still re-renders the chart with thousands of points. Nothing in the chart's path checks whether its props are the same objects as last time, and one of those props is brand new on every render anyway.
The belief: memoization is free insurance. A cache can only skip work, so wrapping every value and every function means React does less, and the worst case is that it does nothing.

Smart developers believe this because the Hooks sound like optimizations and are often taught as one. It's also half true. React's docs say that memoizing everything does no significant harm, and some teams choose to do exactly that so they don't have to think about each case. But "no harm" isn't "faster". The docs list only a few cases where these Hooks help and say there's no benefit in the rest. Meanwhile the code gets harder to read, and the team believes a slow screen is already optimized.

blocks.title: The cache is not a guarantee

content.text: React's docs call memoization a performance optimization, not a guarantee. React may throw a cached value away, for example when a component suspends during its first mount, and a
component may still render. If your code is only correct when the cached value survives, like an object that must be created exactly once, keep it in state or a ref instead. And a custom
must compare every prop, functions included, or the child keeps stale closures from an old render.
